title: Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp.
lead: Fox canceled Shirley MacLaine Parker’s musical and offered equal pay for an Australian western. The court held that the different role and reduced approval rights could not support Fox’s sole mitigation defense, while the dissent wanted a trial on the differences’ practical importance.

actors.name: Shirley MacLaine Parker
actors.role: Actor promised the lead in Bloomer Girl

actors.name: Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corporation
actors.role: Studio repudiating the agreement and offering a replacement role

actors.name: Acting Chief Justice Sullivan
actors.role: Dissenter favoring a trial on comparability

proceedings: Parker obtained summary judgment for $750,000 plus interest. The California Supreme Court affirmed six to one. Rehearing was denied October 28, 1970.
limits: The majority did not decide whether guaranteed pay independently excused mitigation. Fox challenged only rejection of its particular substitute offer, not Parker’s general efforts to find work. The dissent did not hold she necessarily had to accept.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A canceled musical led to a different starring offer
paragraphs: In August 1965, Shirley MacLaine Parker contracted with Twentieth Century-Fox to play the female lead in Bloomer Girl, a musical to be made in California using her dancing and acting. The agreement guaranteed $750,000 for fourteen weeks beginning May 23, 1966, expressed as $53,571.42 per week. It also said Fox need not use her services but must pay the guarantee subject to the agreement’s terms.

On April 4, Fox notified Parker that it would not produce the film or fulfill its obligations. In the same letter, it offered the female lead in Big Country, Big Man, a dramatic western involving an Australian opal mine and filmed in Australia. Compensation was identical, and thirty-one of thirty-four numbered provisions remained. But the new offer eliminated dance-director approval because it was not a musical and reduced director and screenplay approval to consultation with Fox retaining the final decision. Parker had one week to accept and did not.

sections.title: Fox made mitigation its sole defense
sections.cue: Explain why the case reached summary judgment.
paragraphs: Parker sued for compensation due or, alternatively, breach damages. Fox admitted the contract’s validity, her compliance and readiness to perform, and its own anticipatory repudiation. Its only defense was that she unreasonably failed to mitigate by rejecting Big Country. Though she had not begun Bloomer Girl, the parties stipulated for the motion that she had been discharged so wrongful-discharge damages principles applied.

The trial court awarded Parker $750,000 plus interest on summary judgment. Fox appealed, arguing that the substitute offer created a factual issue requiring trial. The governing procedure required adequate moving evidence and no genuine material dispute, with strict construction of the movant’s affidavits and doubts favoring trial. An opponent’s admissions could establish facts, but a party’s own conclusory pleading could not substitute for proof.

sections.title: Comparable employment was a prerequisite to the defense
sections.cue: Explain the majority’s treatment of the undisputed differences.
paragraphs: Justice Burke’s majority stated that an employee ordinarily recovers promised pay less earnings the employer affirmatively shows were received or reasonably could have been received elsewhere. Before unaccepted work can reduce recovery, however, the employer must establish comparable or substantially similar employment. The employee need not accept different or inferior work.

Fox raised no issue about Parker’s general job search. Its defense depended entirely on this offer. The majority regarded a California musical lead and an Australian straight dramatic western lead as different kinds of work. Independently, removal of approval rights made the substitute inferior. Equal pay did not erase those contractual losses.

Fox’s declarations calling the offer comparable and not inferior were conclusions about undisputed terms, not facts creating a triable issue. Recognizing loss of approval rights required neither entertainment expertise nor judicial notice. Once the offer was different or inferior, the majority required no further weighing of whether Parker reasonably rejected it. That resolved this record without creating a rule that every comparability dispute can bypass trial.

sections.title: Sullivan wanted evidence of practical importance
paragraphs: Acting Chief Justice Sullivan agreed that an employee need not take different or inferior work but disputed the majority’s application. Both offers were starring roles; genre, location, and approval rights required factual assessment. The question was the reasonable importance of a lost term compared with the replacement’s advantages. Treating every omitted right as dispositive threatened to eliminate mitigation in practice.

Sullivan observed that Parker’s evidence did not explain the practical significance of approval provisions. Fox’s production executive described her dramatic and western experience, denied reputational harm, and disputed injury from the lost approvals. He also criticized the trial court’s judicial notice of entertainment practices without the opportunity to be heard required by Evidence Code section 455.

He would reverse for a trial on comparability, not order Parker to accept the role. He allowed that summary judgment could be proper where adequately developed declarations established manifestly dissimilar employment.

sections.title: The guaranteed recovery was affirmed on the narrower ground
sections.cue: Preserve the undecided argument and participation.
paragraphs: The majority did not reach Parker’s separate argument that the guaranteed-pay provision and other grounds excused mitigation altogether. The substitute offer’s legal inadequacy was enough. The agreement’s guarantee therefore was not adjudicated as a general waiver of mitigation.

Burke’s opinion was joined by McComb, Peters, Tobriner, and assigned Justices Kaus and Roth; Sullivan alone dissented. The $750,000 judgment plus interest was affirmed six to one. Rehearing was denied October 28, 1970; Mosk did not participate in that denial, and Sullivan favored granting it.
